title: Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
summary: Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC. Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack. “Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.” The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme , the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites. “The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. title: When does cooling an AI processor from inside the silicon improve efficiency?
summary: Engineers can now etch cooling channels into the back of an AI processor and circulate liquid close to its hottest regions. Tests on a working CPU and an NVIDIA GH200 show what this changes for sustained clock speed, GPU temperature and nearby high-bandwidth memory. The electricity question requires a wider view. A retrofit at Lawrence Livermore reveals how much depends on which fans slow down and where the heat finally goes. A separate Berkeley Lab study shows how changing the cooling plant alters the projected savings. Together these results explain when a data centre might serve more AI requests within an existing power limit, which parts of a liquid-cooled rack it could reuse, and what manufacturers must establish about sealed channels, filtration and reliability before deploying the technology across a fleet.

summary: The last week of major security and resilience problems is proof that business and consumer users must think just as deeply about tech resilience as any big enterprise. The pace at which major outages have impacted major entities in the last few days will already have had an impact on business, imposing real consequences. A week IT leaders can’t ignore The incidents are very hard to ignore. Microsoft’s major outage November 12-13 took out Microsoft 365 services for an unacceptable 24 hours , and the FAA grounded US flights for more than four hours on Nov. 13 because of network equipment outages. This week, a JPMorgan Chase outage rippled throughout the financial system, United Airlines experienced a widespread system outage , the US National Security Agency’s classified internal network went down , and then many of Apple’s own systems also hit problems. (Officials do say all these incidents were not connected other than by temporal proximity.) Apple’s big outage saw several of its enterprise and consumer services fail. These included iCloud sign-in and backups, Apple Pay, the App Store, and Apple Support. It also extended to developer services such as App Store Connect and Xcode Cloud and the company’s own internal corporate tools, including AppleWeb. Internal system failures meant physical Apple Store retail operations were also hobbled, disrupting sales, customer pickups, and device repairs. There were reports that device management onboarding was briefly out of action, while others reported errors setting up new iPhones. Apple moved quite swiftly to resolve the problems inside working hours, from when they were first reported at around 11:45 a.m. ET to full restoration at around 6 p.m. ET. So, was it a hack? Apple said it was not caused by a cyberattack and has given no indication that personal data was put at risk. title: A refreshingly practical hidden Gemini treasure
summary: A fascinating contrast is shaping up around us here in the land o’ Googley matters, seemingly more with every passing month. On the one side, you’ve got Google, who’s dead-set on pushing Gemini into every place possible and doing everything in its power to convince us to use it — in spite of its alarming little habit of, y’know, getting stuff wrong . More often than not, the company (like most tech players these days) is also focused on impractical processes and overly complex use cases that few actual humans have any interest in embracing. On the other side sits us — the (allegedly) human mammal-people who are toting around all this technology, often begrudgingly, and mostly just looking for simple ways to make it more useful and simultaneously less intrusive in our lives . With exceedingly rare exception, nearly everyone I’ve chatted with in 2026 shares the same basic sentiment — that AI feels invasive and annoying, that most of what it’s offering has nothing to do with our current wants and needs, and that the type of tech we actually want somehow keeps getting worse as a result of its intrusion. We need look no further than the Google Assistant-Gemini contrast on Android or the frustrating devolution of so-called smart speakers and screens for some all-too-relatable examples. That’s why I, like so many of you, mostly roll my eyes at every new AI announcement and its lack of any real impact on my day-to-day life. And that’s also why I’m constantly on the prowl for ways Gemini can actually be useful when it comes to real-world productivity. Perhaps not surprisingly, the discoveries that resonate the most tend to be the simplest, least flashy features imaginable — and that’s absolutely the case with the genuinely useful Gemini gem I want to share with you today. title: Microsoft adds HorizonDB to Fabric to ease development of agent-driven applications
summary: Microsoft is adding a serverless flavor of HorizonDB to its data and analytics platform, Fabric, to make it easier for developers, business teams and AI agents to build intermittently used applications for automating business workflows and supporting agent-driven tasks. The hyperscaler first unveiled HorizonDB for Azure at its Ignite conference in November 2025, positioning it as a PostgreSQL -compatible database for demanding enterprise workloads, including mission-critical applications that require high performance and scalability. Its architecture, according to Microsoft, combines shared storage with elastic, scale-out compute to support the performance and scalability that large databases and transaction-heavy workloads require. The new flavor, named Fabric HorizonDB , which was launched in public preview at this year’s ongoing Ignite conference, by contrast, targets smaller workloads that do not require continuously running database infrastructure. It provides a managed backend that automatically provisions and scales databases based on demand, pausing them when idle and resuming them when needed, the hyperscaler wrote in a blog post . It also lets applications query live transactional data alongside analytical data in OneLake through a single PostgreSQL interface, reducing the infrastructure and data integration work involved in building applications, it added. In order to support translytical queries, Fabric HorizonDB uses Fabric Data Warehouse’s distributed compute to execute supported analytical portions of PostgreSQL queries across CPU- and GPU -powered resources, while retaining transactional processing in its PostgreSQL engine, it further wrote. New database could reduce engineering effort Analysts, too, see Fabric HorizonDB’s serverless and translytical capabilities helping developers simplify the development of agent-driven applications. “Agent-driven applications often need to spin up databases on demand to support specific tasks and workflows. title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
summary: Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers. Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour. “The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post . The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm. Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack. Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. How the stealer worked The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well. The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. title: Microsoft launches MAI Code 2 models to challenge OpenAI and Anthropic in AI coding
summary: Microsoft has launched a pair of AI coding models that it says can compete with offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, marking its latest effort to build proprietary AI capabilities and reduce reliance on the partners that helped fuel its generative AI push. The two new models, MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash, were launched at Ignite 2026. MAI Code 2 is designed for common enterprise coding tasks such as deep debugging, implementing changes across multiple files, repository-wide reasoning, and user interface development. MAI Code 2 Flash, meanwhile, targets high-volume tasks such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. Microsoft said it built these models to prioritize the coding work its customers do every day. The new models are explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and long-horizon agentic work, the company noted in the press statement. The launch also marks another step in Microsoft’s effort to build its own AI model capabilities and reduce its reliance on external providers. With the launch of new coding models, Microsoft reduces its dependence on OpenAI and Anthropic, said Pareekh Jain , CEO at EIIRTrend & Pareekh Consulting. “Microsoft also has a major advantage through GitHub, Visual Studio and Azure, which are already used by millions of developers. Its immediate goal is to strengthen its developer ecosystem and reduce AI costs. So it doesn’t have to pay OpenAI and Anthropic every time someone uses GitHub Copilot. Microsoft is protecting its profits and locking developers into its own tools,” he added. Microsoft’s models put to the coding test Microsoft compared MAI Code 2 with competing models across four widely used benchmarks in GitHub Copilot: DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1. title: Four major changes coming to Rust
summary: Over its decade-and-a-half lifetime, the Rust programming language has evolved dramatically. Rust has always been about ensuring safe programming with strong typing that doesn’t sacrifice speed. But how it expresses those capabilities has matured and expanded, and that movement hasn’t slowed. If anything, it has accelerated. At any given time in Rust’s development, you could point to dozens of different initiatives to improve the language . As of the end of 2026, four of these stand far above the rest, because of how broad their impact could be and how deeply they touch on many aspects of Rust. The next-generation trait solver Rust’s type system uses “traits” to define the functionality that a given type has and can share with other types. If we described a trait named ExportToJSON , we might have a matching impl , or implementation, for a data type: impl ExportToJSON for CSV The Rust compiler tries to find matching implementations for each reference to a trait. This is highly important for generic functions, since it may not be obvious if an implementation exists for a given invocation of a function. The current version of the trait solver has problems dealing with situations like self-referential types. Those aren’t common, but Rust programmers must consciously avoid constructing them to keep the trait solver from getting tied up in knots. Sometimes, because of this, it’s the developer who gets ensnarled. A new version of the trait solver takes a totally different approach to the problem. It draws on ideas gleaned from an earlier attempt to rewrite the trait solver (called “ Chalk ”), and uses a sophisticated caching mechanism both to avoid problems with self-referential types and potentially run faster than the current solver. The current version of the new trait solver covers some use cases, but not all of them. The next step is to ensure that the solver can cover all use cases, including async features. title: AI agents will soon surpass us
summary: I was talking with my daughter the other day. We made a bet five years ago that I lost. I bet her that by this week non-fungible tokens (NFTs) would be a major part of gaming. I was obviously wrong. She made the point that I don’t know anything about the gaming community, and she’s clearly right about that. She did admit that I was right about one thing — that agentic coding would become the norm. (I wish I had bet her about that instead, but I didn’t see that coming at all five years ago…) Like many young people, she was skeptical about AI in general, and didn’t like the idea of using it to write code. Leveraging LLMs to build games is frowned upon, but her mind was changed when she read about a company that used AI to solve a gaming problem that a Unity engineer told them was unsolvable . Apparently the gaming community considered this very controversial . It would seem that I truly don’t understand the gaming community. While they appear to be concerned mainly about the “harm” that AI is doing, I am far more interested in the fact that AI solved a problem that was considered not solvable. I think we are all going to need to get used to that. Not unsolvable AI has been doing this kind of thing for a while now. Mathematicians have been feeling it strongly, as AI has been solving problems that have stumped us humans . For example, this past May, an OpenAI internal model “ disproved a central conjecture in discrete geometry ,” the Erdős unit distance problem . Now, I’m no mathematician, but “disproving a central conjecture” seems like a pretty big deal. The model’s result wasn’t a complete answer, but it opened a door that humans quickly walked through to a place no one had conceived of yet. Fábio Caversan , the CTO of the Stefanini Group, made a similar point to me recently. “Get used to the fact that whatever you code today will be outdated in six months,” he said. title: Tokenomics Foundation: Making sense of what AI actually costs you
summary: For the last two months, I have been reading and trying to understand more about tokenomics. In my conversations with peers in the industry, I hear the same question more and more: “We’re spending on AI, but what are we getting for it?” Most teams can tell me their monthly bill. Very few can tell me which use drove it. If you’ve ever opened an AI bill and felt your stomach drop a little, you’re not alone. Cost companies now spend real money on tokens, API calls and GPUs. Very few can connect that number to a business result. That’s the gap of the problem the Tokenomics Foundation wants to close. And honestly, it’s about time someone did. Here’s what I found, what it is, what it does and two ideas from it worth knowing. What is AI tokenomics? What I like about this definition is that it doesn’t stop at the token price. In my experience, the price per token is rarely the problem. The problem is how many tokens quietly consume. Every prompt you send and every response you get is split into tokens, and each one costs something. AI tokenomics means understanding that cost structure and connecting it to business outcomes. As a rough rule, one token is about 4 characters, or 0.75 words, in English. AI tokenomics is the practice of managing that economy. The Foundation’s own tagline sums it up: don’t just count tokens, get value from the total cost of AI. That means looking at the whole picture, from the power and hardware that produce tokens to the business value they create. One quick clarification: this has nothing to do with crypto. In crypto, “tokenomics” means the supply and incentives of a coin. Here, it means the cost and value of running AI. Who is behind it The Tokenomics Foundation is a Linux Foundation project that launched in August 2026. It works alongside the FinOps Foundation , which did the same job for cloud spending.
